historical_timeline.summary: Born in San Francisco's Chinatown; raised in Hong Kong from three months old.
Returns to the United States; studies at the University of Washington and teaches gung fu.
Marries; opens a school in Oakland; develops Jeet Kune Do.
His father dies in Hong Kong.
Severe back injury lifting a barbell; months of bed rest and chronic pain afterward.
Films The Big Boss for Golden Harvest in Hong Kong.
Collapses while dubbing Enter the Dragon; convulsions described; cerebral oedema diagnosed and treated with mannitol.
Neurological evaluation with an electroencephalogram finds no abnormality; phenytoin prescribed.
Dies in Hong Kong, aged 32, of acute cerebral oedema after taking an Equagesic tablet for a headache.
Coroner's inquest records death by misadventure; the cause of the cerebral oedema remains disputed.
The Bruce Lee Foundation is founded.

claims.statement: In 1970, without warming up, he lifted a 125-pound barbell in a "good morning" exercise and severely injured his back; after many tests an injury to the fourth sacral nerve was found. He was ordered to complete bed rest, told he would never do gung fu again, and stayed in bed for about six months before beginning his own recovery program; the injury became a chronic source of pain for the rest of his life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern chronic low back pain problem and its pain management. The source is his family's company; the medical details (fourth sacral nerve) are as it reports them.

claims.statement: A nine-day coroner's inquest with testimony from pathologists from several countries followed; doctors at the inquest disagreed about what had caused the cerebral oedema, the medical evidence was insufficient to prove that the drug caused it, and a verdict of death by misadventure was recorded. Traces of cannabis were found in his stomach and intestine.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluation and management after a first convulsive seizure in a 32-year-old Chinese American martial artist, actor and film-maker in Hong Kong, anchored to his documented collapse with convulsions at a film studio two months before his death. The episode covers the emergency care that preceded the index visit (recorded as history); telling a seizure from convulsive syncope (witness history, ECG and QTc); sodium, glucose, calcium, kidney function and creatine kinase; MRI with an epilepsy protocol and a sleep-deprived EEG; classifying the event as an unknown-onset motor (tonic-clonic) seizure by the ILAE 1964 classification and deciding that a single unprovoked seizure with normal studies is not epilepsy; the AAN/AES 1962 guideline on whether to start an antiseizure medicine after a first unprovoked seizure (recurrence risk 21% to 45% over two years, lower with immediate treatment but with no long-term benefit), decided with him in favor of no medicine and a clear plan for a second seizure; triggers (sleep deprivation, heat, missed meals, fluid and electrolyte balance, cannabis); medicines that lower the seizure threshold; Hong Kong driving rules; seizure first aid and work safety for a stunt performer; and his documented chronic back pain managed with exercise and pain medicines that neither lower the seizure threshold nor interact. It is taught with culturally appropriate care: his languages, his philosophy of training, and his own decisions, without stereotype.

documentation.chief_complaint: Epilepsy clinic after a first seizure

hpi.narrative: Bruce Lee is seen at the epilepsy clinic by Dr. Abernathy-Leung eight days after the collapse, with the MRI done this morning and a sleep-deprived EEG this afternoon; he slept about four hours last night, as asked, for the EEG. He has had no further events. A colleague who was with him at the studio confirmed the account by telephone at his request: he came back from the restroom pale and sweating, said he felt faint, sank to the floor, became stiff with his arms flexed and then jerked all four limbs for about a minute with his eyes open, vomited, and was confused and unable to answer questions for about 20 minutes. Nobody saw how the event began. He remembers feeling hot, light-headed and nauseated in the restroom and nothing after that. He had slept about four hours a night for a week, had eaten little that day, had been drinking a lot of water in the hot booth, and had used cannabis that morning. He has never had a seizure, febrile seizures as a child, a serious head injury with loss of consciousness, meningitis, staring spells or jerks on waking, and no relative is known to have epilepsy. The emergency department sodium was 136 mmol/L and glucose 104 mg/dL, and the CT of the head was normal.

assessment_plan.assessment: The prolonged confusion afterward, the minute of rhythmic jerking and the vomiting point to an epileptic seizure rather than convulsive syncope, in which jerks are brief and recovery is quick; the ECG was normal. By the ILAE 1964 classification it is an unknown-onset motor (tonic-clonic) seizure, because nobody saw how it began. No acute symptomatic cause was found: sodium, glucose and calcium were normal and he was not intoxicated or withdrawing from a drug, so sleep loss, heat, missed meals and cannabis are counted as triggers, not causes. MRI and EEG are normal, there was no earlier brain injury and the seizure happened while he was awake, so his risk of another seizure is at the lower end of the 21% to 45% over two years. He does not have epilepsy. Dr. Abernathy-Leung explained that starting a medicine now would lower the two-year risk but would not change the long-term outlook, and that side effects affect 7% to 31% of people. He chose not to start one, and both clinicians agree

Four days ago, at a film studio, he felt hot and faint in the restroom after hours of voice recording in a booth with the air conditioning off, lost consciousness, stiffened and then jerked all four limbs for about a minute, vomited, and was confused for 20 to 30 minutes. consultant_note.history: Bruce Lee, a 32-year-old martial artist, actor and film-maker, is seen at the request of Dr. Cheung-Hartley eight days after a first convulsive event at a film studio. He remembers feeling hot, light-headed and nauseated in the restroom after a long session in a hot recording booth, and nothing more until he was in the ambulance. A colleague, by telephone at his request, describes him sinking to the floor, stiffening with flexed arms, then rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about a minute with the eyes open, vomiting, and confusion for about 20 minutes; the onset was not seen. Triggers that day: a week of about four hours of sleep a night, little food, a large water intake in the heat, and cannabis that morning. No previous seizure, febrile seizure, head injury with loss of consciousness, central nervous system infection, staring spells or jerks on waking; no family history of epilepsy or of sudden death at a young age. Chronic back pain since a lifting injury three years ago; acetaminophen only. He wants to understand the evidence and decide for himself

assessment.assessment: An epileptic seizure. The prodrome of heat and faintness could fit syncope, but a minute of rhythmic jerking, vomiting and 20 minutes of confusion do not: convulsive syncope causes brief, irregular jerks and a quick recovery. The ECG gives no cardiac cause. By the ILAE 1964 classification it is an unknown-onset motor (tonic-clonic) seizure, because its onset was not witnessed and the EEG shows no focal features
Yes, both are indicated after a first seizure. The MRI with an epilepsy protocol shows no hippocampal sclerosis, malformation, tumor or scar, and the sleep-deprived EEG has no epileptiform discharges

An acute symptomatic seizure requires a severe metabolic disturbance, intoxication or withdrawal, or an acute brain insult. His sodium, glucose and calcium were normal, and the cannabis did not amount to intoxication by his account; cannabis is not an established epileptogenic drug. Sleep loss, heat and missed meals lower the threshold but do not make the seizure provoked. This is a first unprovoked seizure. With a single seizure, a normal EEG and MRI, and no earlier brain insult, he does not meet the ILAE definition of epilepsy

Not now, which he chose after hearing the evidence. Adults with a first unprovoked seizure have a 21% to 45% risk of another within two years, and his normal EEG and MRI, daytime seizure and lack of a prior brain insult put him at the lower end. Immediate treatment would lower the two-year risk but not the chance of long-term remission, and side effects affect 7% to 31% of people. A second unprovoked seizure, or an epileptiform EEG on any repeat study, would mean epilepsy and starting a medicine such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine

Hong Kong's licence regulations list epilepsy and liability to sudden fainting among the conditions for which a licence must be refused or cancelled; I advise no driving for at least six months, as many licensing authorities require after a first unprovoked seizure, and then a review. No work at heights, falls or swimming alone until six months; sparring and training are fine once his back allows. No cannabis for now, which he chose. Drink to thirst with salt or an electrolyte drink in the heat, not large volumes of plain water. For his back, avoid tramadol and bupropion, which lower the seizure threshold, and carisoprodol or meprobamate, whose withdrawal can cause seizures; acetaminophen, short courses of an anti-inflammatory and exercise therapy are safe
